Adsorbent / material: SW/Ghassoul (stevensite-rich) and NSW/red clay (illite-rich); alginate (AL), carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), biochar (BC) in eight clay/polymer/biochar bead configurations
Experimental design / conditions: Two Moroccan natural clays; sodium alginate and CMC; biochar from Mentha pulegium plant residue after essential-oil extraction. Main text gives pyrolysis for 2 h at 550 °C with minimal oxygen; finer preparation details are referenced to SI.
Reported result: Eight configurations were compared: SW+AL, SW+AL+BC, SW+AL+CMC, NSW+AL, NSW+AL+BC, NSW+AL+CMC, AL and AL+CMC.
Model / metric: Material preparation; adsorption/desorption study; characterization plus computational interaction analysis
Caveat / follow-up: Do not classify all items as unmodified biopolymer; clays, polymer-only and BC composites are distinct material classes. SI not supplied.

Adsorbent / material: Natural clays and composite beads listed in E01
Experimental design / conditions: Batch adsorption/desorption, 0.5 g sorbent in 10 mL solution, 24 h, 25 ± 2 °C; applied SDZ 0–40 μmol/L; solutions prepared in 0.005 M CaCl2.
Model / metric: Batch test; retained-quantity and adsorption-ratio equations
Caveat / follow-up: Additional preparation and statistical details are in SI, not supplied.

Adsorbent / material: SW and NSW natural clays; SW+AL; SW+AL+BC; SW+AL+CMC; NSW+AL; NSW+AL+BC; NSW+AL+CMC
Experimental design / conditions: At applied SDZ = 40 μmol/L the paper reports SW 173.89 μmol/kg (21.7%); NSW 110.64 μmol/kg (13.83%); SW+AL 250.52 μmol/kg; SW+AL+BC 237.88 μmol/kg; NSW+AL 431.94 μmol/kg (53.99%); NSW+AL+BC 171.14 μmol/kg; NSW+AL+CMC 387.25 μmol/kg; SW+AL+CMC 800 μmol/kg described in body text as 100%.
Reported result: Quantities and percentages as reported at this test point; do not treat as a common set of fitted saturation qmax values.
Model / metric: Observed retained quantity/adsorption ratio at specified starting concentration
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2 Table 1; PDF p. 4 §3.2; Figs. 2–3, PDF pp. 5–6
Caveat / follow-up: 800 μmol/kg at 40 μmol/L is exactly the solute inventory in 10 mL divided by 0.5 g: 0.4 μmol/0.0005 kg. It is consistent with complete removal under that test, not a verified fitted saturation qmax.

Experimental design / conditions: Composite tests describe pH ~5.74–9.84; cited SDZ pKa1=2.7 and pKa2=6.4. The paper describes increasing anionic character above pH 6.4 and decreased uptake in some configurations as pH rises.
Reported result: Several material/solution-pH comparisons are reported; for SW+AL+CMC a decline from 800 to 173.89 μmol/kg is described in a pH comparison, while NSW-based comparisons vary differently.
Value / units: pH ~5.74–9.84; pKa 2.7 and 6.4; reported amounts μmol/kg
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 4 §3.2; Fig. 1 PDF p. 5; supporting Figs. S6–S7 referenced
Evidence status: Main PDF verified; supplementary data pending
Caveat / follow-up: Material pH and solution pH are distinct in the paper; do not collapse multiple configurations into one universal pH curve.

Experimental design / conditions: Paper states Freundlich, Langmuir and linear models were fitted; Freundlich generally matched best with R² 0.87–1 and often lower errors. Kd reported 1.42356–7.77179 L/kg for most samples, exceptions NSW+AL+CMC=19.28732 and AL+CMC=294.169 L/kg.
Reported result: Freundlich generally preferred; Langmuir errors are said to be too large in nearly all instances. Suggested interactions include ion exchange, π–π, electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonding.
Model / metric: Freundlich/Langmuir/linear fits and computational interaction interpretation
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 6 §3.3; PDF pp. 5–8, Figs. 1–3 and §3.4; SI Table S9 referenced
Evidence status: Main text verified; fit tables pending
Caveat / follow-up: Supporting model tables in SI were not supplied; mechanistic pathways should be stated as author interpretation, not independently proven causation.

Adsorbent / material: Natural clays and composite beads, especially CMC-modified systems
Experimental design / conditions: Text reports lower desorption for CMC-modified composites, including 0% for SW+AL+CMC and 3.51% for NSW+AL; raw clays exceed 10% in some comparisons.
Reported result: Reported low desorption: 0% and 3.51% for the named composites. Abstract separately states “more than 100% adsorption”, while methods define ratio as (C0−Ce)/C0×100.
Value / units: % desorption; claimed >100% is invalid unless explained, and no explanation is given
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 8 §3.5/conclusions; Figs. 2–3 PDF pp. 5–6; abstract PDF p. 1; Eq. (2) PDF p. 3
Caveat / follow-up: Conclusion phrase 'desorption less than 0%' is incoherent with its 0%/3.51% results. Do not use >100% adsorption or negative desorption as physical findings; 800 μmol/kg must not be ranked as fitted qmax.

Target / co-contaminant: Pharmaceuticals; antibiotic examples include erythromycin, clindamycin and clarithromycin
Adsorbent / material: Seed-waste biochar SW (500 °C); pine/spruce mainly bark PS (production details undisclosed); sewage-sludge biochar SS (600 °C, ~25 min); forest-biomass FB (500–800 °C, ~3 h); spruce SP (650 °C, ~10 min)
Experimental design / conditions: Five biochars used in original form after drying at 110 °C for 16 h. Table 1 lists average packing masses SW 41±4.1 g, PS 21±1.8 g, SS 104±4.1 g, FB 76±0.5 g, SP 16±0.6 g.
Reported result: Five feedstock-specific biochars compared under flow-through conditions.
Value / units: Temperatures/times and packing masses as reported
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2 Table 1 and §§2.3–2.4; PDF p. 3 §2.3
Caveat / follow-up: PS production details explicitly not disclosed; do not infer a uniform preparation route or rank without accounting for packing, pore properties and conditions.

Target / co-contaminant: 42 non-spiked pharmaceutical targets and 16 spiked compounds; antibiotics include erythromycin, clindamycin, clarithromycin
Adsorbent / material: Five biochars from E01 packed in duplicate PVC columns
Experimental design / conditions: Tertiary effluent from Uppsala municipal WWTP (sand filtration, activated sludge and FeCl3 flocculation); flow 12 mL/h; 1 Feb–16 Dec 2024 (~45 weeks, ~635 bed volumes). One scenario spiked 16 pharmaceuticals at 100 μg/L; other monitored 42 non-spiked target compounds.
Reported result: Long-running column test on actual tertiary effluent with native and controlled spike scenarios.
Value / units: 12 mL/h; ~45 weeks; ~635 BV; 16 spiked at 100 μg/L; 42 non-spiked
Caveat / follow-up: Not a controlled single-solute test; influent concentrations varied and only a subset of the target compounds could be modelled due to LOQ/variability.

Adsorbent / material: SS sewage-sludge biochar, FB forest-biomass biochar; SP spruce biochar as poor-performing example
Experimental design / conditions: Authors describe SS and FB as high-retention materials through 635 bed volumes and state “>99%” removal while parenthetically printing “C/C0 >0.01”. SP had complete breakthrough around 20 bed volumes; its columns were measured to 137 BV due to high breakthrough.
Reported result: SS and FB are described as highest-performing overall; SP complete breakthrough at ~20 BV.
Value / units: Bed volumes and C/C0; no qmax
Model / metric: Aggregate median breakthrough curves; Yoon–Nelson 20% breakthrough estimate
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 4 §§3.1–3.3; Fig. 2 PDF p. 5; conclusion PDF p. 9
Evidence status: Main PDF verified; source inequality caveat
Caveat / follow-up: To mean >99% removal, C/C0 should be <0.01; the printed > sign is inconsistent. Aggregate result covers pharmaceuticals beyond antibiotics and possible biofilm contribution.

Adsorbent / material: SW and PS for erythromycin curves in Fig. 4; all five chars within study
Experimental design / conditions: Main text names erythromycin, clindamycin and spiked clarithromycin; Fig. 4 plots erythromycin C/C0 against bed volumes for SW and PS, with a Yoon–Nelson line marking 20% breakthrough (C/C0=0.2). Spiked clarithromycin is described as a larger molecule with high retention.
Reported result: Antibiotic-specific curve evidence exists, but numerical fitted parameters are in absent SI Table S5. No qmax can be extracted from the curve.
Value / units: C/C0 vs bed volumes; C/C0=0.2 threshold
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 7 §3.4.2 and Fig. 4; SI Table S5 referenced
Evidence status: Main PDF verified; SI parameters pending
Caveat / follow-up: Broad pharmaceutical-column study, with antibiotics a subset. Do not infer mg/g capacity from breakthrough curves.

Adsorbent / material: Biochar columns in real tertiary effluent
Experimental design / conditions: Authors discuss influent variability, biofilm formation, biodegradation, desorption/leakage and competition as processes changing the outlet C/C0. No significant visible clogging or pressure buildup was observed after maintenance precautions.
Reported result: Measured outlet reduction cannot be attributed exclusively to adsorption; biofilm-related biodegradation may lower output, while saturation/desorption can raise it.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 4, 6–8, §§3.1 and 3.4.1–3.4.2; conclusion PDF p. 9
Caveat / follow-up: Use as long-term application evidence; no isolated adsorption mass balance, regeneration experiment, cost analysis or LCA is reported.

Adsorbent / material: Magnetic activated carbon (MAC) made from paper-mill primary sludge; KOH-activated base PAC magnetically functionalized with iron oxide
Experimental design / conditions: Dried sludge impregnated with KOH at 1:5 KOH:sludge w/w and microwave pyrolysed at 800 °C for 20 min; washed with 1 M HCl and distilled water to neutral pH; fraction <180 μm used; magnetic iron oxides added at pH 5.5 with PAC:iron oxide 3:1 w/w.
Reported result: Waste-derived activated carbon was modified for magnetic separation/recovery; activation, acid washing/neutralisation and magnetization are part of the process.
Value / units: 800 °C, 20 min; KOH:sludge 1:5; 1 M HCl; PAC:iron oxide 3:1
Caveat / follow-up: Not pristine biochar. Full production details partly refer to earlier work; do not assume unreported yield, cost or energy inventory.

Experimental design / conditions: Batch tests 250 mL, 25.0±0.1 °C, stirred at 500 rpm, triplicate. Kinetics at 0.05 mg/L SMX used MAC 1 mg/L in ultrapure water vs 65 mg/L in WWTP effluent, 5–360 min. Isotherms used 0.02–1 mg/L initial SMX with 3 h contact. WWTP effluent was 0.45 μm filtered; pH 8.2, conductivity 6.9 mS/cm, DOC 10.4±0.1 mg/L; sample from one plant/campaign in July 2023.
Reported result: Directly tested SMX adsorption at lower concentrations in a filtered real-effluent matrix, but dose differs substantially by matrix.
Value / units: 0.02–1 mg/L isotherm; 0.05 mg/L kinetics; MAC 1 vs 65 mg/L; pH 8.2; DOC 10.4±0.1 mg/L
Caveat / follow-up: Filtered effluent from one WWTP is not untreated wastewater or multi-plant validation. Different dosages must stay explicit in matrix comparisons.

Experimental design / conditions: At [SMX]i=0.05 mg/L, 25 °C, MAC 1 mg/L (ultrapure water) versus 65 mg/L (effluent); stirring from 5 to 360 min. Table 2 reports experimental qe for the selected doses.
Reported result: Equilibrium about 180 min in ultrapure water and 60 min in effluent; experimental qe 20.3±0.8 mg/g in ultrapure water and 0.25±0.01 mg/g in effluent.
Caveat / follow-up: Unequal adsorbent dose (65 vs 1 mg/L) changes the qe basis; the faster equilibrium time is not an equal-dose comparison. Better model fit does not prove the mechanism.

Experimental design / conditions: Langmuir/Freundlich fits to 0.02–1 mg/L initial SMX, 3 h contact; dose 1 mg/L ultrapure water and 65 mg/L effluent. Authors say the effluent data do not form a clear plateau.
Reported result: Langmuir qmax 54±2 mg/g in ultrapure water vs 6.2±0.3 mg/g in effluent; Kd 1296±170 vs 9.3±0.8 L/g. Authors state an 83% qmax reduction, but 54 to 6.2 mg/g is ~88.5% by arithmetic.
Evidence status: Main PDF verified with model/calculation caveats
Caveat / follow-up: Effluent qmax is model-derived rather than a measured plateau. Preserve source's 83% statement as a flagged arithmetic discrepancy rather than silently correcting it.

Experimental design / conditions: Effluent pH 8.2, conductivity 6.9 mS/cm, DOC 10.4±0.1 mg/L. Authors attribute poorer adsorption to dissolved organic matter competition and electrostatic repulsion at effluent pH.
Reported result: Derived Kd in effluent is over two orders lower than in ultrapure water, indicating lower low-concentration affinity in that matrix.
Model / metric: Author interpretation based on derived distribution coefficient
Evidence status: Main PDF verified with attribution caveat
Caveat / follow-up: This is the authors' explanation for a single effluent campaign, not an independently isolated causal test across different WWTPs.

Experimental design / conditions: Loaded MAC dried at 105 °C then microwave-pyrolysed at 700 °C for 20 min under N2; four regenerated materials prepared. Reuse tests used 0.05 mg/L SMX and MAC 1 mg/L in ultrapure water or 65 mg/L in effluent.
Reported result: Effluent removal 41±2% fresh MAC and 26±6% at Regen-2. Authors report removal reductions of 66% in ultrapure water and 85% in effluent after the third regeneration. SBET declined 42% after Regen-3; W0 decreased 40%; Vp 36% lower than Regen-2; Table 4 gives SBET 622 m²/g for fresh MAC vs 5 m²/g for Regen-4.
Model / metric: Microwave thermal regeneration and reuse; texture/magnetic characterization
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 3 §2.5.2; PDF p. 7 §3.3/Fig. 4; PDF p. 8 Table 4/Fig. 5
Evidence status: Main PDF verified with regeneration caveat
Caveat / follow-up: Conclusion describes satisfactory performance up to two cycles, but the effluent removal has already dropped from 41±2% to 26±6% at Regen-2. Retain both statements; repeated high-temperature treatment damages the porous/magnetic structure.

Experimental design / conditions: Laboratory adsorption and regeneration; no pilot-scale validation or cost/LCA analysis is reported in this paper.
Reported result: Authors list environmental impacts/LCA of production/use/regeneration and off-gas, pilot-scale validation and reliable techno-economic cost estimation as future work.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not cite this paper as having demonstrated lower lifecycle cost or full environmental superiority; these are future assessment topics.
